context_heading: Understanding chemical peels and choosing safely
context: A chemical peel uses acids to remove damaged outer layers of skin, which can improve texture, tone, acne, and fine lines. The depth of the peel affects how much downtime you need, and your skin type affects whether a peel is suitable at all. Sun protection afterwards is vital to protect healing skin.

Chemical peels are not prescription medicines, but they are still cosmetic procedures. In England, the government has set out plans for a licensing scheme for non-surgical cosmetic procedures, but until that is in force you should choose a clinic carefully. Practitioners on registers such as Save Face or the JCCP, and doctors and nurses registered with the GMC or NMC, offer extra reassurance. Clinics run by regulated healthcare providers may also be registered with the CQC.

faqs.q: Is a chemical peel safe for all skin types?
faqs.a: No, suitability depends on your skin type and the depth of the peel. A practitioner should assess your skin in person before recommending a peel.

faqs.q: How much downtime will I need after a chemical peel?
faqs.a: Downtime varies with the depth of the peel. Superficial peels may cause slight redness for a short time, while deeper peels can involve more noticeable peeling and recovery.

faqs.q: What should I do to protect my skin after a peel?
faqs.a: Sun protection is vital after any chemical peel, as your skin will be more sensitive. Your practitioner should give you specific aftercare advice.

faqs.q: How do I choose a safe practitioner for a chemical peel near me?
faqs.a: Look for a practitioner who assesses your skin in person and explains the risks and aftercare. Checking whether they are on a register such as Save Face or the JCCP, or are a doctor or nurse registered with the GMC or NMC, can offer extra reassurance.
